answer.label: Not Mother Teresa — an anonymous coda on Kent Keith’s poem
answer.authorName: Kent M. Keith (poem) — the coda itself is anonymous
answer.authorDates: Keith b. 1949 · American author of the “Paradoxical Commandments” (1968)
answer.sourceLine: Mother Teresa did not write this line. It is a two-sentence coda grafted onto Kent M. Keith’s “Paradoxical Commandments” (written 1968) sometime between 1995 and 1999 — and per Quote Investigator and Keith’s own site, Keith says he did not write the coda and dislikes it. Mother Teresa merely had a version of the commandments posted on a wall of her children’s home in Calcutta, which is how her name became attached.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: People are often unreasonable, illogical and self-centered; Forgive them anyway. … Give the world the best you have and it may never be enough; Give the world the best you have anyway. You see, in the final analysis, it is between you and God; It was never between you and them anyway.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the whole set to Kent M. Keith’s 1968 “Paradoxical Commandments” and notes “sometime between 1995 and 1999 a coda was added” — the very “final analysis” lines — in its study Do Good Anyway.
Keith’s own site, The Mother Teresa Connection, states the final “analysis” lines were added by someone else and that they “trouble” him.
Mother Teresa’s link is a wall sign reproduced in Lucinda Vardey’s 1995 book A Simple Path, which readers misread as her own authorship.
source.excerptNote: The closing two sentences (the “final analysis” coda) are the disputed line. They were not in Keith’s 1968 original and were added anonymously between 1995 and 1999.
source.rightsNote: The underlying “Paradoxical Commandments” are Kent M. Keith’s 1968 work (in copyright), but this specific coda is an anonymous addition that appeared between 1995 and 1999 with no identifiable author, so no clear rights status can be asserted for the line itself.

author.name: Kent M. Keith
author.kicker: The real author of the poem
author.heading: Kent M. Keith
author.metaLine: b. 1949 · American author & speaker · wrote the “Paradoxical Commandments” in 1968
author.bio: Kent M. Keith wrote the ten “Paradoxical Commandments” in 1968 as a 19-year-old Harvard sophomore, publishing them in a booklet for student leaders titled The Silent Revolution. Decades later he learned a version had hung on a wall in one of Mother Teresa’s homes in Calcutta, and in 1997 he wrote the book Anyway expanding on the commandments. Keith has publicly stated that the popular “final analysis” ending was not written by him and troubles him because it can be read as justifying giving up on other people.

misattribution.heading: How Mother Teresa got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” misattribution: an anonymous line attached to a poem that itself was never hers.

items.why: The ten “Paradoxical Commandments” were written by Kent M. Keith in 1968, long before any Calcutta connection. A version hung on a wall in her children’s home and was reproduced in Lucinda Vardey’s 1995 book A Simple Path under the heading “Anyway,” which readers mistook for her own words.

The “in the final analysis… between you and God” ending was not part of Keith’s original poem. Per Quote Investigator it was added anonymously between 1995 and 1999, and Keith himself disavows writing it.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is Kent Keith’s poem; the specific line is an anonymous coda — and Keith says neither the coda nor the poem was authored by Mother Teresa.

context.heading: Why this one spread
lead: The full poem — often retitled “Anyway” or “Do It Anyway” — became a viral inspirational text long before social media, precisely because it was believed to be Mother Teresa’s. The wall sign in Calcutta was real; what got lost was that the words on it were an American college student’s from 1968.
The closing couplet is the most-quoted fragment, yet it is the part that is least anyone’s: an unsigned coda that even Keith, the poem’s author, says he did not write and would not have written.
context.pull: The sign was on her wall — the words were never her pen.
